utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, you wanted to raise a matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I just wanted to take a few seconds to update the Trial Chamber with the position for this week, if I may. I appreciate that there are witnesses here, so I won't take too long in that. First, as I told the Court last week, we're ready to file our exhibits today. We'll try to do that during the break. We have them here, five copies for the -- three for the Judges, one for the registry, one for the OTP. Each of these exhibits, booklets, has an index. It looks daunting, but about 50 per cent of them are actually the separate tabs, so it's fairly easy to follow. In addition today, we have filed under seal, for the reason that some of the witnesses have testified in closed session, our designation of transcripts. I think there are six of them from prior cases. With respect to the batting order for the rest of the case that the Prosecution had requested, I trust that the Court has received that. We faxed it to the Prosecution on Saturday, so now they know which witnesses we would like to call for the remainder of the case. One matter that I did want to take up. We had agreed yesterday, after preparing to do this, to allow the Prosecution's audiotape expert to testify after Mr. Koenig. We had requested a curriculum vitae and I had thought that Dr. Broeders was in fact a technical expert, but apparently he's not. He does not actually address any of the issues that Mr. Koenig raises. He's a linguistics expert. He does not have a scientific background in audiotape analysis, and that is a little bit of a problem. At least, that's what it appears from the curriculum vitae that I was given about a minute ago by the OTP. With respect to the witnesses for tomorrow, there are two witnesses who will testify in open session: Mr. Neimarevic and Ms. Vidovic. The outlines have been prepared and distributed. The other witnesses, two of them are not yet in The Hague; two are. And as soon as their outlines are prepared and signed and reviewed, we will distribute them to the Prosecution. And I think that basically brings the Trial Chamber up to speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, in relation to the exhibits and the transcripts, a suitable time must be found in which their admissibility can be discussed. If there's any objection, no doubt that can be towards the end of your case, and perhaps in the last week we could look to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In relation to the witnesses -- I've a copy of the fax, June 30th -- eight witnesses are set out. Those are the witnesses for this week, I take it, ending with Mr. Jelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, as far as the Prosecution witness is concerned, if they wish to call him, are you objecting to his being put forward? What is the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm not exactly sure what the witness is going to be testifying about. I had thought that he was a rebuttal expert that the Prosecution wanted to move up for reasons of convenience --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- so that the Court could hear all of the evidence. But I do not believe that he actually rebuts the technical analysis that Mr. Koenig is here to testify about today, because he doesn't have any technical qualifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a matter for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So if the Prosecution wished to call the witness, you would have no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. That's proposed to take today, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, but I would point out, Your Honour, that this is essentially a rebuttal witness, so any time taken in direct and cross-examination should be deducted from the time allocated for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It won't be held against you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But that is the proposed plan today?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And then you've got two witnesses for tomorrow, 2 and 3 on your list.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And you can deal with the other five in the rest of the week; that's the schedule?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I would think so. With the exception of perhaps one witness, all of these witnesses are relatively short. They're brought here to address discrete issues in the case, Mr. President, and I don't anticipate we would be more than one hour with any one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the -- let me see. You say that you provided a copy of the rest of your witnesses. Is that the schedule which is attached?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There's an identification of the remaining witnesses, I think, at the end of our fax of July 1st, Your Honour. If you'd give me a minute, I can locate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps we can have a copy. Maybe one has been sent through and just hasn't reached us. But tell me, how many more witnesses have you got after these eight, after this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The week of July 10th, Your Honour, one witness testifying here live, perhaps two; and three witnesses by videolink, perhaps four, but probably three. And perhaps it might be that we would take the afternoon of Wednesday of that week before the Plenary Session to address the matter of exhibits, or that can be left for the next week if the Trial Chamber wishes. On the week of July the 17th, which is the week that we anticipate closing our case, we would finish -- or at least I hope to finish one witness who has previously testified, Witness DK, but I have to tell the Court that we have not been successful in getting hold of him to date. Then the second witness that we identified, we probably will try to call in the week of July the 10th, live, right after the first witness. And then there are three other witnesses, two of whom are questionable, one of whom is definite. And that would -- we still anticipate finishing before the end of that week, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That sounds a relatively short week.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Shall we call the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I just make two points, I think, or three. First, we are indebted to the Ministry of Defence for Dr. Broeders' attendance here today -- Minister of Justice, I'm sorry. Wrong ministry. There was no way that we could, through United Nations arrangements, secure his attendance here, because he was supposed to be in Rome. His ministry, in order to assist the Tribunal, has taken care of the financial consequences of the change of his plans, and we're grateful to them for that. The second point relates to the order of witnesses for this week. We were notified about the complete change of order after I had left The Hague at about 5.00, I think, on Friday. I haven't been able to prepare myself for the change of witnesses. It may be, if we don't have a natural break between the expert witnesses and the first of the witnesses to be called, I'd be asking for a short adjournment to deal with that. And as to the last week, the 17th of July, I have yet myself to see the letter that has been faxed, but it will come to my attention soon. I've been told who one of the witnesses is on that week, a potentially important witness, and I would be asking if that witness does arrive, that he be not started before the Wednesday because of my commitments to be elsewhere on the Tuesday. We've also sent a letter to the Defence a copy to yourselves dated the 30th of June which deals with the batting order of witnesses, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you will be in a position to deal with the exhibits and the transcript witnesses as early as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. I've got to see what quantity of material is involved and how much work's going to be required of my team but yes, of course, as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you could let us know what the position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Mr. Koenig, could I just of all have you state your full name for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, my name is Bruce E. Koenig, K-o-e-n-i-g.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And Mr. Koenig, could you explain to the Court the number of times you've testified as an expert in the area of audiotape analysis as well as an idea of the jurisdictions in which you've been qualified as an expert witness in that area.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This would be my 320th time to testify as an expert in the field of audio and video analysis. I have testified mostly in the United States, in 42 of the 50 states, the District of Columbia, Guam, Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands. I've also testified in the Turks and Caicos Islands in the Caribbean.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And have you testified for the Prosecution as well as the Defence in various cases?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Could you explain your -- the positions that you've held with the Federal Bureau of Investigations and the length of tenure you spent with the FBI?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I came on board as a special agent of the Federal Bureau of Investigations in late 1970. After finishing my training, which lasted about 5 months, I was assigned to the Atlanta, Georgia office and then following that, the Detroit, Michigan office where I investigated various crimes consisting of bank robbery, selective service violations and fugitives. In 1974, I was promoted to a supervisory special agent position in the FBI laboratory, the engineering section of that, where I remained until 1995 when I retired. During the time I was in the laboratory, my full-time position was conducting audio and video tape analysis examinations, supervising people in that field. When I finished managing, for the last five or six years, the entire group of about 30 or 35 engineers and technicians and scientists.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: What was the specific name of the group that you managed at your retirement from the FBI?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: It was called the Audio/Video Signal Processing Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And can you explain the nature of what that group did and the size of that group and that laboratory?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The group was responsible for conducting examinations of audio and videotapes for things like enhancing the intelligibility, comparing voices, determining the authenticity of audio and videotapes, conducting signal analysis examinations of things such as gunshots and airplane crashes, and any other related areas. The FBI's laboratory was then and still is by far the largest in the world. In fact, it's so large that it's much larger than all other governmental and private labs in the United States put together. On an average year, they'll look at over 3.000 recordings to determine their authenticity or enhance them for various other functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Can you please explain your work history after retiring from the FBI?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. After retiring, for the last four-and-a-half years, I set up my own business and also have several associates with the same background as mine that are involved in conducting the same types of exams I did at the FBI. My clients include the Federal Bureau of Investigations, Office the Independent Counsel, Department of Justice, numerous private attorneys, corporations and other clients.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Can you give us an idea of the equipment available within your laboratory as a consultant?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I modeled my laboratory after the FBI's, so it consists of professional audio and video recorders and specialised units. For instance, professional microcassette playback units, special types of analysis equipment, digital filtering equipment, high-end computer systems with specialised software and other related equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: How many years total experience do you have analysing audio and videotapes?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Twenty-six years full-time experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Can you give us an idea of the number of tapes you've examined over that 26 years with respect to audio and video tape?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Somewhere between 12.000 and 13.000 tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And what is the total number of criminal, civil, and administrative matters that you've been involved with that have raised issues concerning audio or video tape analysis?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Between 4.500 and 5.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: On your curriculum vitae, you make reference to doing work with respect to independent counsel investigations. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber the nature of your work for the independent counsel and what that entity is?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: The Office of Independent Counsel was set up as an Act of Congress to assist the Department of Justice in specialised types of investigations of government employees. This was done, I believe, for political reasons. Mostly to make an it an independent analysis outside the government of such violations. I've worked on two major investigations of that in the last few years. The first one involved the secretary of the government, a man named Henry Cisernos, who was Secretary of Housing and Urban Development which is called HUD, involving various violations, potential violations of the law. In that, his paramour at the time produced 88 tapes of various conversations between the two of them. She stated that these tapes were all original and unaltered. The government came to me and asked for my evaluation in which I determined that all 88 tapes were copies, in fact, most were copies of copies. And many of them contained various alterations. The second case I worked on, major case I worked on with them, involved the case against the President of the United States, William Clinton, and allegations by various people involving his relationship with Monica Lewinski. In that matter, I analysed a number of tapes made by an individual named Linda Tripp of her conversations with Monica Lewinski. Parts of my results are still sealed, but the parts that were not were my findings that many of the tapes that were identified as being original were, in fact, copies and to date, the government has not located the originals of those tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Koenig, with regard to this affair, what was the outcome? Was your determination accepted?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Ultimately, the woman that made up the tapes ended up with a three or four year gaol sentence, and Mr. Cisernos agreed to plea to just a misdemeanour and was fined a small amount of money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: You have also been involved, according to your curriculum vitae, with analysis of acoustical information concerning the assassination of President John Kennedy. Can you explain that analysis or your involvement with regard to that specific project?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Back in the late 1970s, there had been several congressional groups that had looked into the assassination and the subsequent investigation. This group came up with certain individuals who claimed that there was a second gunman involved based on an acoustical analysis of a police department radio traffic recording. I, along with my associates at the FBI, were asked to look into this and we were able to determine that, in fact, there was no evidence of any gunshot sounds on that tape whatsoever including the original shots that we knew were fired or from a second shooter. Subsequent to that, the analysis was also performed by the National Academy of Sciences which is, in my opinion, the most prestigious scientific group in the United States, and they concurred with our results and, in fact, came out even stronger than that in fact the original scientific analysis had been done in a very poor way and had no validity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Did your work on that project result in any publication?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. My original work for the FBI was published by the Department of Justice as a separate document and I subsequently published a peer review article concerning the work of the congressional committee, the work of the FBI and the work of the National Academy of Sciences review.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Could you summarise for the Trial Chamber your formal educational background?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I have a bachelor of science degree from the University of Maryland with a double major of physics and mathematics. I've completed an electronics course through De Vry Institute of Technology in Chicago. I have a master's degree from George Washington University, which is located in Washington, DC in the field of forensic science. I've taken additional graduate level courses in my area of expertise at Massachusetts Institute of Technology, the University of Utah and George Mason University.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Could you give us an idea of your publications in this field?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I've published over 25 peer reviewed articles and a large number of administrative type of articles for meetings. My peer review articles appeared in a number of journals including the Journal of the Audio Engineering Societies, Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, the Journal of Forensic Identification and the Crime Laboratory Digest.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: I believe you were involved in drafting comprehensive standards on spectrographic voice identification. Could you explain that publication as well as the nature of spectrographic voice identification.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes. Spectrographic voice identification is a non-conclusive but meaningful examination conducted in what we call forensic analysis. That is, investigative kind of tapes, to compare a voice on a tape to a known exemplar. The FBI has been operating under stringent standards since probably the 1950s, but most other people in the field at the time that I was called in to write the standards were operating under either no standards or very loosely defined type of standards. The International Association for Identification asked that I come in and be involved and write such standards. I did do that. The standards were then approved by the members of the International Association for Identification subcommittee involved in this matter, plus the parent group. They were subsequently published and are now probably the major source of standards in this field.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Before we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask Mr. Koenig: When you speak about analysis allowing you to distinguish the original of a particular audio recording and the copy, do you also take care of the alterations? Do you take note of the alterations, and are you then in a position to establish the exact difference between the original and the copy? If you are examining a copy, for instance, what has been added to it, changed, modified, that is, what you call alterations, does that mean that you can see the change that has been introduced as against the original or into the original?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Your Honour. As background and authenticity examination first off must be done on the original recording, to be meaningful, and when it is, three areas are determined. One is: Is the tape original or not? And in my field we define "original" as a recording that was made simultaneously with the information on the tape. That is, there's a telephone call; the recording was made at the exact time of that telephone conversation. Second, you determine if the tape was stopped or started at any place during the original recording process. And third, was the tape subsequently edited in any way? If you only have a copy, you cannot do a meaningful examination. You're very limited to what you can do. However, if you have the original and a copy, then an examination can be made to determine: Is the copy an accurate reproduction of the original? But you would have to have the original to do that examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Mr. Koenig, before we address the body of your report and the conclusions and findings that you reached, perhaps it would be beneficial to cover some background with regard to audiotapes and how they are actually created. Could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Browning, bear in mind that we've had the witness's report and we've had the chance to look at that, so you can take the matter more quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Mr. Koenig, could you explain the components of the tape recorder that are significant in understanding your report, and specifically if you could explain erase heads and record heads and how they work within a tape recorder, please.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: An analog tape recorder, for instance, like for cassettes or microcassettes, basically does two functions, no matter how expensive or cheap it is. One is it transports tape at a standard speed and electronically takes a signal and records it and will play back whatever is on the tape. As part of the recording process, standard cassettes and microcassettes have two magnetic heads. The first is a record-head. This head is used to write the information onto the tape, moving it from an electrical signal to a magnetic signal on the tape. The other head is an erase-head, and that head erases whatever was on the tape previously. From a physical perspective, these two heads are spaced apart. For instance, on a standard cassette, the spacing is usually slightly more than an inch apart, because they have to fit into the front of the housings of the tapes. So one head, as you're recording along, is writing the information, and the head before it is erasing anything that was there prior to this recording. And these two heads are spaced physically apart, again, as I said, because they have to fit into the front of the housing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Now, when you performed your analysis in this case, you requested a copy, a digital audiotape copy of the Prosecution exhibits at issue here. Could you explain what a digital audiotape copy is?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Digital audiotape, or normally called a DAT, D-A-T, is a professional digital format that is heavily used throughout the world in the professional audio field and the forensic field and allows you to make virtually a perfect copy, if done properly, of an analog tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: If I could ask the usher to distribute an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's this supposed to be, Mr. Browning?

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the transmittal of the digital audiotape that was made for Mr. Koenig, and I wanted him to confirm that it was recorded in a manner in which he had requested. If it's possible to have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be numbered D287/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How did you come across this? This is a -- seems to be a document written inside the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: I believe it was provided to us by the Registrar when we had asked for the digital audiotape to provide to Mr. Koenig and confirmation that it was recorded by analog cable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I think it would have been better to have raised this with the Court, if you proposed to put internal documents into evidence, Mr. Browning, as a matter of courtesy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. When it was provided to us, I assumed it was provided so that we could have confirmation of the way in which the tape was recorded. And that's all that I was trying to establish, that the tape that the witness was provided was provided in a way in which he had requested. And I would be glad to withdraw the exhibit and simply ask the witness if he received information that the tape was recorded by a synch cable analog to a Sony DAT.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Why not deal with it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Mr. Koenig, the digital audiotape that you examined, was it your request that the digital audiotape be recorded by a synch cable analog to a digital audiotape and recorded at 44.1 kilohertz?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Turning to the first page of your laboratory report, you refer to the digital audio tapes that you received, and designated one as Qc4, and that tape had the bearing T000-456; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: I think you left a zero out. T000-0456.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And the Prosecution, for ease of reference, has referred to that copy as Prosecutor Exhibit 2801.4.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And you also received a second digital audiotape which you designated as Qc5, and the label on that tape was T000-0331; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And for ease of reference, the Prosecution, in its filings, have referred to that as Prosecutor Exhibit 2801.1. When you received the digital audio tapes, how did you physically store and handle those tapes?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: My facility has been accepted by the US Department of Defence as a top secret facility clearance, so therefore I am allowed to store and analyse top secret material. So even though this was not a classified matter, I stored it in an identical way; that is, I have a safe file, approved by the Department of Defence, and a locked area with alarms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And how was the tape marked by you when you received it?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: I marked it with either Qc4 or Qc5, the two tapes, my laboratory number, and my initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And that was actually physically marked on the tape at the time you received the tapes?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: On the tape housing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: What's the reason for marking tapes such as that?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: This is a standard procedure that I have been taught, both as a field agent and as a forensic examiner, to be able to identify a particular recording in the future. Since I handle so many tapes, there would be no way for me to identify a particular recording without having markings on it that tell me exactly what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And your examination of the digital audiotape recordings was performed in the United States in your laboratory?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Can you explain how an audiotape is examined for authenticity?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: If a tape is an original tape, there's a series of listening and instrumentation and physical examinations that are conducted of it. They're usually broken down into seven areas that you use to conduct, to make your decisions regarding originality, continuity, and alterations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And I believe you had previously indicated that an authenticity exam can only be done with an original tape.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: You have an original tape and you do an authenticity exam. What are those seven steps, if you could explain those, please.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Critical listening, which is a four-step process of carefully listening to the tape by playing it back on professional equipment and listening on headphones. In my field, nobody uses loudspeakers. Everything is done through headphones. Physical inspection, which is involved with looking at the tape itself to ensure that there's no physical changes to it or splices, determining that it's the right length. For instance, a C-60 audio cassette should run approximately 30 to 33 minutes per side. Magnetic development, which is an analysis in which a ferro fluid is placed on the tape and allows you to visualise the actual pattern on the tape. Narrow-band spectrum analysis, which is an analysis of the frequencies on the tape. And by "frequencies," I'm referring to, for instance, like a musical instrument. The lower notes would be lower frequency and the higher notes would be higher frequency. High-resolution wave analysis, which is a display of time versus amplitude or volume of the signal, and it's exactly how everybody is hearing, everybody else here today. We listen to sound waves. This allows us to blow them up and have much greater detail. The sixth one that's potentially used is called spectrographic, which is a display of both time, frequency, and amplitude, all in one graph. And lastly, like most other fields of expertise, you have to have a miscellaneous one, so miscellaneous is rarely used, but there are some types of analysis in this field that do not fall clearly within the other six areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Now, with respect to a copy as opposed to an original, I take it that many of the steps you just ran through cannot be, as a practical matter, performed on a copy of an audiotape?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Which steps, if any, is there some benefit to performing with respect to a copy of an audiotape? And specifically, if you could focus on the steps that you took with regard to the tapes that you were provided.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. You're normally limited down to just a few types of exams, and even within those areas, you're limited to what you can do compared to an original tape. But in this case I did do critical listening, high-resolution waveform analysis, and narrow-band spectrum analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And with respect to critical listening, can you explain what you were able to discern about these tapes based upon critical listening?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: There was a number of things that were obvious on these tapes by listening. One is that they're representative of one or more acoustical copying steps. And by "acoustical copying," I mean that the information was played back through a loudspeaker, probably a very small one, and then recorded into another tape recorder through a microphone. That's different than cabling it from one tape recorder to another one. Second, that many of the conversations you do not hear the very beginning and end of the conversation or the telephone hook-up; that in a number of places it sounds like the recording was stopped or started; that the quality, overall quality of the tapes was relatively poor, and in fact at times difficult to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And with respect to narrow band spectrum analysis, can you explain how that analysis was performed on these tapes and what you were able to learn as a result of that analysis?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I analysed the information of these tapes using a device called an FFT in which it breaks down the component frequencies. By doing so, I determined that there were no indications that it was -- the tape recorders being used were plugged into the wall using what we call AC power and that much of the information was probably consistent with battery operation. Also, the tapes, though it was difficult to tell because of the copying process, seemed to be consistent with the limitations of a telephone system.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: I want to focus for a while upon the high-resolution waveform analysis and what that allowed you to learn about the tapes that you were provided. And let me first of all ask you to explain what a record stop signature is, that I believe you refer to in your report.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. A record stop signature, in my field, refers to the sounds made by the tape recording system when you stop a recording normally by pressing the stop button while the tape recording is in progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Does that produce a -- can that be heard, actually on the tape by critical listening?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Not as in much detail as you can reflect in the waveform graphs, but certainly most stop signatures on cheaper tape recorders produce signals that are aurally obvious to the listener.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Do different tape recorders produce different record stop signatures?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And is there a difference generally between a microcassette stop signature and a regular cassette record stop signature?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The reason they are different is for two reasons. One is the standard cassette and the microcassette run at two different transport speeds, that's how the tape moves within the housing. And second, the spacing that's allowed within the housings, the microcassette and standard cassette have very different housings, that allow where the heads can be placed, changes the spacing between them. So the overall effect is you get different spacing between microcassette and standard cassette record stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: If I could ask the usher to distribute an exhibit, please, and if I could ask that they be given two different numbers, please. If I could first of all ask the registrar for the number for the regular cassette, the larger one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And for the second exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Mr. Koenig, if I could ask you first of all to turn to D287/1, the photocopy of a regular cassette. If you could explain this exhibit and particularly the placement or where a record-head and erase-head will come into contact with the tape when it's played in a cassette -- when it's placed in a cassette recorder.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This exhibit shows a picture of a standard cassette with a ruler beneath it. Where the "E" is will reflect where the erase-head would go into the housing and the "R" would be where the record-head would go into the housing at that point. They are approximately 2.7 centimetres apart in this particular picture. There can be some slight variance within that based on the particular tape recorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And so the signature that's left on a regular cassette recorder is a factor of the distance between the erase-head and the record-head as well as the speed at which the tape is played?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And if you could turn to D288/1 and explain the placement of the record-head and erase-head with respect to a microcassette?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: A microcassette tape runs in the opposite direction of a standard cassette, that is, right to left. And in this you can see that the record-head placement has been placed at zero on the ruler, and the erase-head at approximately 8 to 9 millimetres away from it and the spacing kind of below near the "A" on the tape itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: What is the speed at which a microcassette will run?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Standard speeds are either 1.2 or 2.4 centimetres per second.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And the speed at which a regular cassette runs?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: 4.8 centimetres per second.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the usher to distribute an additional exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D289/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Mr. Koenig, if I could ask you to briefly explain what you have before you.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. These are --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have them on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't know that you're going to get much out of it on the ELMO. Perhaps the witness could explain it so the interpreters could follow and so the Court can follow too.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. These are time wave forms of a number of events. They all represent eight tenths of a second, the horizontal access. The vertical access represents amplitude or volume of the signal and the number "A", and the letters are in the upper right-hand corner. "A" would represent a test stop on a microcassette recorder running at 2.4 centimetres per second.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Before we turn from that page, if you could focus on that example of a microcassette record stop signature. Could you explain the grouping of lines on the left portion of page A to Exhibit 289/1?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The portion, that very small portion, it's like a half an inch long on the left side, represents the end of the recording and the stopping of the record-head writing the information on the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: So on the left is the actual signature of the record-head?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The record-head signature with the information that was in the recording up to that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And then does the erase-head signature appear on this page as well?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It appears in the middle of the graph and takes up two to three inches in the middle of the graph.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And this event, page A on Exhibit 289/1 is an event that can actually be heard with the human ear?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And the -- well, first of all, let me ask you, on this specific page on this example of a microcassette record signature, what is the speed at which this microcassette is running?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: It's running at 2.4 centimetres per second.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And if you could turn to page B and briefly explain this page.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir, this is another time waveform. This is a test stop on a microcassette recorder running at 1.2 centimetres per second and, in fact, it is the same recorder as the one used for the 2.4 centimetres per second.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And again, the grouping of lines on the left will be the information for recording record-head engaged and the signature of the record-head, explain to me the grouping of lines on the left-hand portion of page B?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Again, this would represent the recording coming up to the point where it stops and the very end of that information on the left would be the record-head itself's signature of stopping.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And the waves appearing towards the right-hand portion of page B, what does that indicate?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: That's the erase-head event.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And if I could ask you to turn briefly to page C. Can you explain what this page is?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This, again, is a time waveform of a test stop on a cassette tape recorder running at 4.8 centimetres per second. Again, on the left side, is the information leading up to the record-head stop which is a bigger event than on the left, and then three-quarters of the way across the page, that two or three inches of information is the erase-head event.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And taking these examples of a microcassette record stop signature versus a regular cassette record stop signature, pages A and B, would that be a signature that would be distinct and different from page C which is the regular cassette?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The -- again, each tape recorder might have slightly different signatures on the actual thing, but the spacing would be approximately the same for each of these. So therefore, the spacing on microcassette recorders when they stop is different than the spacing on a standard cassette when it stops.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: You have included test examples of a microcassette as well as a regular cassette, but could you explain what a minicassette is?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: A minicassette is actually a different format made by Phillips that has not been used in the United States for approximately 15 years, and in most of the world. However, I think it is available in many places in the world so a lot of people -- that is the actual format, but my experience has been that many people who say it's a minicassette, that's a very common term in the United States, for instance, actually you are referring to a microcassette. So the format actually exists although it's quite rare now, but microcassettes are very dominant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And in one would look to a record stop signature for a minicassette which is what you've referred to is cassette manufactured by Phillips which is rare, how would the minicassette record stop signature look in comparison to either a microcassette or a regular cassette?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: It would certainly look different than a regular cassette depending how the heads are formatted in that particular unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And just like a microcassette or a regular cassette, a minicassette would have a distinct record stop signature?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: If a conversation is recorded using a microcassette recorder, will there be a record stop signature on that recording?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Well, I guess you have to look at the point that if you start recording, you always have to stop. So, therefore, there must be a stop some place on the tape although it could be very at the end of the side which at times can be difficult to playback properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And that would be if -- well let me ask you this: The typical time for a microcassette runs for how long?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: It would depend on the length of the tape. The most common microcassette would be a MC-60 which means, depending on the speed you're running at, would run something over 30 minutes or something over 60 minutes per side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: So if you are using a microcassette recorder and allowed it to run to the very end of that 30 or 60 minutes, then it might be difficult to discern a record stop signature at the end of the microcassette?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: The answer is yes. The stop would exist there but at times it could be difficult to playback without specialised equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: But if you are using a microcassette and are recording with a microcassette and stop it short of the end of the tape, you would expect to see a record stop signature on that microcassette?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And if the entirety of that microcassette is then taped onto a regular cassette would that microcassette signature then be copied onto the regular cassette?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, I would expect on a copy to see a copy of the original microcassette stop probably followed by the original stop of the copying tape recorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And on the tapes that you examined, there was no indication of a microcassette stop signature or was there?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: There was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Now, I take it there could be numerous explanations for why a microcassette stop signature does not appear -- let me back up. If someone is taping a conversation using a microcassette recorder and then makes a copy of that, I take it there are numerous reasons why the microcassette stop signature isn't -- is not transferred onto the copy, numerous potential explanations?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And one explanation would be that the micro -- a microcassette was not originally used after all?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that would be one explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And one potential explanation, I take it, is that the microcassette stop signature could have been edited out either intentionally or unintentionally?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And I take it another potential explanation is that there was no record stop signature on the original microcassette if, for example, it had been recorded over?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Another potential explanation, I take it, would be that the entire microcassette was not copied onto the regular cassette?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And then the final explanation, I guess, is what you described previously, that the record stop signature could be at the very end of the microcassette and would make it very difficult to discern?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. There is a little bit of explanation there. By that, I mean in my laboratory we have specialised tape recorders, we can play it back, but average person would not have such a tape recorder. So if you try to play it back, it might not playback the end stop signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Is there -- the tapes that you were provided for examination, is there anything on those tapes to indicate that the original was recorded using a microcassette recorder?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And is there -- the tapes that you were provided, is there anything on those tapes to indicate to you that the original -- original conversations were recorded using a minicassette?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Can you summarise the conclusions that you came to as a result of performing a high-resolution waveform analysis on the tapes you were provided?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I was able to determine through the stop events that there is at least three and possibly four different cassette tape recorders used to record the information on the tapes I was provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And is it possible that even more recorders were used to create this tape?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It's possible that some other stop events, if they ever existed, could have been erased or recorded over by the present information on the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: So there is an absolute minimum of three regular cassette recorders involved in producing the tape that you examined?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And there is a possible indication of a fourth regular cassette recorder involved?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And there may, in fact, be others that you weren't able to determine from your analysis of the tape, as you said, other record events could have been masked some how, record stop events?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: That's possible, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Now, the stop signatures that you are referring to, are those the result of a recording event or are they the result of a playback event and could you explain the difference?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: First, they are the result of a record event, that is a recorder is recording and was stopped. When you play back a tape, you can certainly get transients from the playback system, and playing it back especially on cheaper tape recorders. But these events were reflective of a tape recorder recording and then stopping.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Now, if I could ask you to turn back to Defence Exhibit 289/1, and if you could explain pages D through I of this exhibit, please. If we could start with page D.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: This exhibit again is another time waveform, lasting 8/10 of a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And forgive me for stopping you, but this waveform was taken from your high-resolution waveform analysis of the tape that you designated as Qc5, which would be Prosecution Exhibit 2801.1.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: This event occurs at 2 minutes and 58 seconds from the beginning of the recording and reflects a stop event, where the record-head over on the left, where you see the kind of a big straight line, sticks up, and the erase-head, or what's left of it, is towards the right side of the graph as a spike that goes down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And does this page D indicate a -- what type of tape recorder does this indicate?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: This represents a standard cassette. The spacing between these two events is 0.580 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And this is one of the regular cassette recorders that you were able to identify the record stop signature when you analysed Qc5?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: If you could turn to page E and first of all explain what this page is and particularly how it differs from the previous record stop signature we saw on page D.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Again this is a time waveform, same spacing of timing of 0.8 seconds. This is another record stop, obviously probably a copy because of all the kind of squiggly noise in here. This spacing is 0.553 seconds. And if you look back at the Exhibit D, you can tell it even looks quite different. It's obviously a different tape recorder than was used for the event D and my event 2 minutes and 58 seconds in. E occurs 15 minutes and 57 seconds into the recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And if you could turn to page F and explain this page, and particularly how it differs from the earlier pages D and E.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: This event occurs approximately 6 minutes and 21 seconds into the tape and has a spacing between the record and erase heads of approximately 0.548 seconds. And again it's consistent with a standard cassette, but it's different somewhat in shaping and also in spacing than the events that are on the graphs D and E. So this is a different tape recorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: So if you compare D, E, and F, if I understand your testimony, these waveform analyses reflect that at least three different regular cassette recorders were used in preparing or creating this tape.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And if you could briefly explain the relationship of pages F, G, H, and I.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. These all have approximately the same spacing of approximately 0.546 through 0.548. So they very well could be the same tape recorder. And these would be events at 16 minutes and 51 seconds in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And that would be page G?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Page H is 4 minutes and 39 seconds in, and I is 8 minutes and 39 seconds. Additionally, and that's why I said there's a possibility of a fourth, F and G are a very good match with each other, and H and I have somewhat different pattern designs than F and G and it's possible they're a different recorder. However, the spacing between recorder and erase-head are virtually identical with F and G, so therefore I was not willing to say it was definitely a fourth recorder, but it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Now, you had explained earlier in your testimony how you were provided with a digital audiotape recording. Would the fact that someone had to take the Prosecution exhibit and make a copy of that on a digital audiotape, could that explain one of these three or possibly four recorder signatures?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: No, sir, for several reasons. First off, the digital audiotape is a professional format and does not leave such signatures, and it would certainly not be consistent with this type of signature even if they did. Second, I had prior recordings provided by your office made on standard cassettes that I went back and looked at, and they were consistent with those two. So these are definitely consistent with what is on the tape possessed by the Court in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: If you were to assume that the original recording of these conversations was made on a microcassette, and if then you were able to ascertain record stop signatures for three or possibly four tape recorders on the tape that you were provided, would that be indicative of a multiple-generation copy of the original tape?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: It would depend. We certainly have three or more recorders involved, so these could represent multigenerational copies in the sense that portions of them are copied from one copy and different portions onto a second copy and then a third and a fourth copy; or they could represent the parts of microcassettes or other tapes being copied onto this tape the Court has with different tape recorders used to make the recordings; or a combination of both of them. And now, since we have a copy, it's not possible to determine that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: See if I've got your evidence, Mr. Koenig. Would you help us. What you appear to say is this: First of all, there's no support for the assertion that a microcassette recorder was used. Secondly, it's not possible to authenticate the copy of a recording, but only the original. Thirdly, that in this case there are three or more recorders used for making these tapes, and therefore it's possible that they were spliced, or something of that sort. Is that going too far or not? I mean, I want to know what the conclusion you're asking, or it may be the Defence in due course, will be asking us to draw.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: I agree with your statements, with two slight modifications. One, even though I see no indications of a microcassette on these tapes, is it possible that the original was a microcassette? The answer is: It could be, for all the reasons the Defence attorney mentioned. Your comment at the end that I'm saying they're spliced is probably wider than I would be willing to state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, that is very much a layman's term, obviously, but I mean all it really amounts to is that the tape may have gone through a number of copies.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What explanation? It's simply copied a number of times?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Portions are, because these stop events occur not at the end, where you might see a bunch of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: They occur in between the conversations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So it's -- I'm sorry to interrupt, but it's not a case of the whole tape being copied as a whole, but copied -- is this right -- bit by bit?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: That would be one explanation, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That would be one explanation.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But although this explains the tape, at the end of the day we're going to have to decide on the evidence what happened.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: You have the much harder job, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Browning, it's coming towards the break. If you can bring the examination to a close, that would be useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: I think I will carry over slightly beyond the break, but we are to the point of wrapping up before long, and I'll leave it to the Court whether now is a convenient time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Take another -- we started slightly late, so take another five to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: In your report you note that, "copies must be viewed with a high degree of suspicion." Can you explain that statement and the ways that someone can go about altering a tape so that it is not discernible on a copy of that tape?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: First off, my thing of suspicion is more from a scientific aspect, and the Court has to certainly look at things like chain of custody, you know, if somebody involved with this conversation is vouching for it, somebody who was there when it was recorded, many other aspects, legal aspects and investigative aspects that I have no knowledge of, or little of. And it's just suspicious from the point of view of a scientist who can authenticate an original tape but cannot authenticate a copy. The ways of altering a tape are numerous. From what I've heard on this tape, the two likely ways, if it was altered, would be either the tape was physically edited in a way to move information around on it, or the more likely scenario in the modern world is the use of a computer with a sound card and certain types of software programmes that make it very easy to manipulate data on a tape. Additionally, these tapes contain a considerable amount of noise and distortion which would mask any editing attempts, if they occurred, on the tape and make it very difficult, even for someone like myself, to be able to discern that editing has occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: You had made reference to computer programmes that are available to allow one to edit a tape. Can you explain those computer programmes, how they work, and to what extent are they readily available.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They are very readily available. I bought a sound card and it had an editing programme, a kind of a -- not a sophisticated one, but an editing programme came with my computer sound card. The programmes are used heavily in the music, radio, and television and other media areas. Every time you listen to a radio or TV show or commercial, or even a song, it most likely has been quite heavily edited. No, we don't listen to it and detect that. In fact, we might even like the effects of the editing. So the programmes are readily available. To give you an idea, I use a professional editing programme in my laboratory. It's one that's very heavily used in the United States, probably the most heavily used in the professional field, and it costs $400. I've seen programmes that were quite good that could be downloaded free on the Internet. So the access to these programmes is pretty universal at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Would you expect that electronic warfare sections of military --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I suspect that's a matter of comment. Unless the witness can give us information about the former Yugoslavia in 1993, I don't think it's going to be a great deal of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Could you explain to us why it's so important to have the original when you do an authenticity examination? What is it that you can do with an original that just can't be done with a copy?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Well, the reasons are numerous, I have to tell you, but I can certainly name a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Some exams cannot be done. You cannot check for physical splices on a copy, because if you physically splice the original copy, they're not there anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Are there other ways that physical examination can be important other than simply checking for splices?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Certainly. You want to know that the length of the tape is correct; if it's a C-60, that it actually runs 31, 32 minutes a side. You can check things like the batch number from the manufacturer to determine when that tape was made to see if it's consistent with the time period involved. So certainly there's a lot of things you can look at physically. Magnetic development, which is one of the most important examinations you can conduct, which visualises the actual track on the tape -- for instance, if you look at a tape you have at home, a cassette tape, pull it out and look at it, you don't see anything. This allows you to see the track by putting the solution on it, which doesn't hurt the tape. That exam you cannot do because it's a copy. The information you're looking for on the track existed on the original but it is not copied over to the copy. Additionally, a lot of events that may be important or in actuality are not a problem can be easily resolved on original tape. For instance, seeing, where I see here, three different tape recorders or more, on the original tape I could determine absolutely how many tape recorders were involved. I wouldn't be coming to the Court saying it's three or more; I'd be saying it is exactly this. When noise or distortion, like we have on these tapes, is present, if it's on the original and it makes sense, it's the original tape, then you realise that's what the original input signal sounded like. When you hear it on a copy, you don't know if that's been added in the copying process, whether it's been added for negative reasons, in the sense to cover up something. Or if you see noise in certain areas but not others, is that consistent with the copying process of the original? You have no way of knowing. And like I said, there's just a number of things you look at. Narrow-band spectrum. If somebody told me it was a battery-operated tape recorder and I found information that reflected it was plugged into the wall, if it's the original tape, that could be very important information. But once I have a copy, I don't know if that information came from the copying process or was in the original tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Are there other examples where narrow-band spectrum analysis will assist you if you have the original to examine, but that same sort of analysis is not as beneficial with regard to a copy?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. There's a lot of those. For instance, if you have a phone conversation, the frequency limits of phone calls is very well behaved because the phone companies set them up in certain ways. Once you make a copy, that can be distorted in ways that makes such analysis useless.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Let me focus on magnetic development.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That may be a convenient moment to break.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Browning, would you look to tailor, please, the rest of your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: I hope to wrap up very shortly after the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Koenig, I warn you, as I warn all witnesses, please don't speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over. We'll adjourn for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Browning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Mr. Koenig, before the break we were discussing the sort of tests that can be performed on an original audiotape but cannot be performed on an audiotape copy. And I'd like to specifically focus what can be done with regard to magnetic development of a tape but before you do so, can you -- you've discussed record stop signatures. Can you explain what a record start signature is?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It's the signal that occurs when you start recording on a tape. That is, the tape sitting there not moving normally, and you press the record and often the play button together to start it recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And can you please explain, with respect to record start signatures, the difference in analysing those when you have an original tape versus a copy of the tape?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Record start signatures are not as unique as stop signatures, normally. Often the erase-head event is erased in the main record signal. However, with an original tape, that information is normally present when you develop it with magnetic development. So therefore, you actually see the start of the erase-head which is initiated through magnetic development, but normally that information is lost and what you actually hear and what is copied from the original to another tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: So as a practical matter, when you have an original, you can look for signatures for record start events, but you generally are unable to do that when you are working with a copy of the tape?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Well, you'll see characteristics of the start, even on the copy, but they're not normally unique enough to be able to say, like I did on the stops here, that there is a number of different recorders involved. Most of the information is lost in the copying process.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Are there any other significant pieces of information that magnetic development will allow you to ascertain on an original but you're not able to use as readily when you're working with a copy?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: There is certainly a wealth of information that magnetic development can tell you; things like matching to a particular tape recorder, determining if what you think is a record event, for instance, a stop or a start is really truly a record event. All that information is lost when you make the copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Mr. Koenig, if I could ask you, you may have in front of you but -- the report of Mr. Broeders, do you have that handy, and there's one specific question that I want to ask you.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: If you could turn to section 3.2.3.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Mr. Broeders appears to be summarising your report and states, "There is direct substantiation in the form of the presence of replay transients for the statement for the original recordings were made on a microcassette recorder." Could you please comment upon that summary of your opinions and conclusions?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe he inadvertently left out the word "no", that is, "there is no direct substantiation". And the word "replay transients" is not a word I normally have seen in my field, but I presume it means transients produced when you play something back. And in my report, I didn't talk about such transients but actually what happens when you are recording on a tape recorder and stopping it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Would you please explain the procedures that are undertaken when you receive audiotape evidence or -- an entity such as the FBI receives audiotape evidence, and what is done with regard to storage and handling and why that is so significant?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The FBI and most of the major law enforcement agencies I deal with treat all evidence, and especially evidence like tapes, very carefully, simply because you could have a tape and erase it and without listening to it, it wouldn't look any different. Or you could make -- have an original and two copies of it all on the same type of tape, same brand. Without marking them, you would not know which one was the original and which one was a copy. So therefore, they usually will mark things like initials, dates, case numbers, many agencies actually mark "original" on the tape, they write it right on there. And more importantly, they store it in a way, often in the United States, it's an envelope that lists when it was recovered, who from, the date it was made, and then the envelope itself has the chain of custody. The original person has it, signs for it. If that person ever gives it up, he or she signs it over to someone else so they sign and the new person signs and they put the date and the time and the reason for the transfer. So everything is right on an envelope which makes it very convenient to always know what it is, who's had it throughout the whole history. And like a lot of cases it's many years sometimes from the time you record a particular conversation to the time it may be used at a judicial proceeding. So all of these are put that way. Where it's stored is also very important. For instance, magnets on things like loud speakers and other equipment can erase parts of tapes or all of tapes on there. So like I said, it's very difficult without playing a tape back and knowing what you had to start with, you just can't look at it and say what it is. I can't pick up a tape here and tell you just by looking at it, telling you if it has a recording on it. I have to put it into a tape recorder and listen to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: The report that was filed with the Trial Chamber, is that a full and accurate summary of your opinions and conclusions in this matter?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Concerning those particular tapes, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And that report incorporates, by reference, an article that you prepared?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir, an article that was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And in that article you cite several different examples of when authenticity examinations are typically performed.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Could you give me some examples of when authenticity examinations are conducted by agencies such as the FBI.

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The person that made the tape and had custody of it dies, or is unable to testify because of illness, or the person's whereabouts are unknown. The government often comes to us when they have a tape that was made by the government; however, it might have blank areas on it; or for some reason there was a problem with chain of custody; tapes in which a tape is given to the governmental agency and the governmental agency is unsure of its authenticity, maybe because the person that gave them the tape has a lengthy criminal record; or other problems that might make his or her testimony in court, the reliability of the tape, not very acceptable to a jury or a judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: I take it that would also apply when there's bias or motive by the person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Browning, this is a Tribunal of professional Judges. I don't think we're assisted by going through what are fairly obvious points.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Mr. Koenig, can this tape that you were provided be authenticated?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: No, sir, because it's a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: If someone has reasonable resources and a sufficient number of voice samples and is given a general instruction to -- as to the sort of thing they would like a tape to say, is it possible to pick and choose from those voice samples and put together a tape that will audibly sound like a true and genuine conversation?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: And if that tape is then copied over, is there any way to determine whether that altered tape is genuine or not?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: No, sir, not in the laboratory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: If someone is familiar with principles of forensic analysis of tape recordings and someone wants to propound a tape that has been altered in some way, would you expect that person to submit a copy or an original?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: They would always submit a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We don't have any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Koenig, your last substantial answer -- I'll just read the question to you again by Mr. Browning: [as read] "If someone has reasonable resources and a sufficient number of voice samples and is given a general instruction to -- as to the sort of thing they would like the tape to say, is it possible to pick and choose from these voice samples and put together a tape that will sound like true and genuine conversation?" You said, "yes" to that. It's not in your report, is it?

utterances.speaker: BRUCE KOENIG
utterances.text: That was a hypothetical question. It wasn't part of my analysis. So the answer is no, it's not in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
