utterances.text: I just wonder, Mr. President, if I could ask the witness whether there's any scientifically compelling reason why a microcassette recorder would be used as oppose today a regular cassette recorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Can you think of any reason, Mr. Broeders?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: They are usually battery operated but that's not a scientific reason that's a practical reason, and they are small.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, keep the interpreters in mind, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I actually have it tuned to channel 5, Your Honour, and I will try to do a better job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Listen to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, with important conversations, such as these are reputed to be, can you think of any reason why an electronic warfare officer would prefer to make copies of the originals rather than keep the originals of these conversations, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: I have no idea but, I mean, I -- this would be pure speculation and I'm not sure that it's a good idea for me to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. All right. Your understanding then is that the microcassette conversation or one of them was recorded on to a regular cassette and then Mr. Husic used that same cassette to record other conversations that were recorded by microcassettes?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: That's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But you would agree with Mr. Koenig that we don't know whether that is actually the case or not because there are no microcassette stop or start signatures on any of the tapes, either of the tapes given to you.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: I have not found any positive evidence for this change of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So scientifically speaking, from analysing the tapes that you were given, that's one conclusion that we can definitely reach. There is, in fact, no direct substantiation for the version of events told by Mr. Husic which is that these conversations were originally recorded on microcassettes and then subsequently rerecorded on to regular cassettes?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: With the reservation that I haven't looked at the entire tape, that's the -- the parts that I have looked at, I haven't found any, but I think it's important to add that I wasn't looking for them because the question I was asked was slightly different.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. You weren't asked to look at that particular path of analysis, were you?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: No, my comments in my report are simply based on the remarks made by Mr. Koenig in his report. I was asked to comment on that so that's why I was talking -- why I wrote about microcassettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And Mr. Koenig did do such an analysis and we've heard his conclusions that there is no evidence on the tapes of the use of microcassette recorders, and you do not disagree with that is what I hear you saying.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: I can't disagree. I mean I can't agree or disagree with things I haven't looked at myself so I can only repeat what I have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you, you said that you looked at a JPS-60 cassette tape, that was one of the two tapes given to you and I believe that that actually had an index, a handwritten index?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. I wonder if we could have you take a look at that index. I think the tape is 2801.3. You've just been shown the handwritten index, Mr. Broeders it's been marked as Exhibit 2801.3. It records 11 conversations on side A, correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: It just says 1 to 11, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And records three conversations on side B, correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. I notice that the dates on the second, third and fourth entries have been changed. Do you know who changed those dates?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: I have no idea. I mean, I wouldn't like to immediately agree that they have been changed, but if you say they have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well why don't we put that on the ELMO and we can all see for ourselves. If I could just ask the technical unit to zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. It looks like entry number two said something different from February 22nd originally, and someone's written over it, the number 22 on there. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: I'm not an expert on handwriting analysis. I wouldn't like to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you notice this when you were looking at the index to this tape?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: I must say that I didn't pay a lot of attention to the writing partly because I was primarily interested in what was on the tape rather what was written on the inlay card.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But certainly, sir, you would agree that you would expect to find 11 conversations on side A, and 3 conversations on side B?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose one would.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And if it turned out that there were not, in fact, 11 conversations on side A, and, in fact, that there were not three conversations on side B, that would be one additional reason to view this particular tape with some suspicion, wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Well, what actually happened was that we made a similar sort of discovery in the sense that, as I think I also indicated in my report, it appears that what is here listed, what are listed as two separate conversations sound, on the tape, like one single telephone call.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: To whom?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: To whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: To whom do they sound like two separate calls when --

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: They sounded to me like two separate calls and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But certainly the person that wrote these down would know whether they were separate calls or not?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You just don't know, do you?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: I'm saying not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: But what I could add is that it is not unusual for people in a telephone conversation to take over from each other and for other people to appear on the phone. I listen to hundreds of telephone taps every year and these things are very, very regular events.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to suggest to you, Mr. Broeders, that there are, in fact, ten conversations on side A, and there are actually four or five conversations on side B which is considerably different from what this index indicates. Now, armed with that information, that would be certainly something that you, as an independent expert, would find to be peculiar, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. You're putting some hypothesis to the witness which it may be that he doesn't even agree with the element that you put at the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me see if I can fill in the gap, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you provided with a copy of the testimony of one of the employees of the Prosecution, Mr. Alihaji Kamara who testified in this case on February 25th?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: I think I've tried to list all the material I received in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kamara actually stated at 15060 of the transcript that there were, indeed, ten conversations on side A and four or five conversations on side B, not eleven, as listed on side A and three, as listed on side B. So let me suggest to you, sir, that those are, indeed, the facts and they throw considerable doubt upon the accuracy of the document that you have before you on the ELMO. Wouldn't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that's fair for an audio expert. This is a matter for argument before the Trial Chamber. The witness is dealing with the tape itself and the conversations on it. You can address us, Mr. Sayers, about these discrepancies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But this -- well, this tape was provided to the expert for an examination, Your Honour, and it's certainly material to the question of integrity which this witness has addressed, whether the listing on the contents of the tape are as listed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've made your point now let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, did anybody impose any time limits upon you to perform whatever test you felt to be appropriate on the audiotape, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You refer, on page one of your report, to the availability, anyway, of an audiotape authentication and integrity examination and you say that the preliminary integrity and authenticity examination was carried out. Did you, in fact, perform any scientific tests upon these tapes, any at all?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Which ones?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: What we did was we tried to -- again, we did an analysis of the tape, the JPS tape as well as the Fuji tape concentrating on the sort of -- I mean actually literally following the procedures that are described in Mr. Koenig's paper, starting from listening and concentrating on the four conversations that the Prosecution seemed to be primarily interested in trying to find whether there was any evidence in any shape or form of tampering in these recordings. And that means, to make matters a little more concrete, that, for example, you do look at the time signal which is, in fact, a sort of picture that Mr. Koenig was showing this morning. So that's a time signal, a direct representation of the speech signal which will show you any stop or start signatures if they are there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you make any records relating to these time signals that you examined?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you listed them in your report?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you make any record relating to your examination of the --

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yes, I -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I wonder if we could request copies of that, Your Honour, to allow Mr. Koenig to look at while I am covering other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the witness has it with him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I have some time signal pictures. I'm not sure that -- again, I think you have to understand that the investigation that I carried out concentrated on those four conversations. So in other words, I did not perform a full-fledged authentication examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, I wonder if we could just take a look at what you did do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just before -- what is it, so that we can follow what you are going to challenge what Mr. Broeders found. What are we leading up to? It would help to know what the area of dispute is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't know that there is a tremendous area of dispute. It appears that there is a wide degree of convergence regarding Mr. Koenig's and Mr. Broeders' conclusions. If I can just -- let me just press on if I may, Your Honour, and I'll try to wrap this up within a half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The fact of the matter is that you -- and you admit this, did you not do a detailed full forensic examination of the type that Mr. Koenig did?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: I'm not sure exactly what Mr. Koenig did, because all we have is a three-page report and six pages of prints of a time signal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But you agree that you did not do a full-fledged integrity authenticity examination?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Koenig's article outlines seven separate steps to do a full-fledged audiotape forensic analysis, and I think you agree with the scientific principles articulated in his article?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The first is that you need to do a physical inspection of the tape itself for the reasons articulated by Mr. Koenig and obviously that could not be done here because there simply isn't an original; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, I mean there could even be splices in a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There could be, but you didn't see any evidence of that, did you? And we don't know whether there were any splices in the original because we don't have the original.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. So we couldn't do a physical inspection of the original. The second thing is a waveform analysis, and we know that you did not do that; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: I did do a waveform analyses of parts of the tape that I looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And what did you conclude? That there were three or four, at least, cassette recorder decks present, and that's the conclusion that Mr. Koenig reached. You agree with that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yes, but the crucial difference is that -- and this is a point I need to stress. There should not be confusion about what we mean by "recording." What we have is a tape, is a compact cassette with what appear to be a number of telephone conversations that are recorded on that cassette. Now, you can call the entire cassette one recording, okay. That's very confusing. The important thing is that the stop signatures that Mr. Koenig has found I think are only between conversations, okay, so there are no replay transients, there are no click reflexes, there are no signatures found within what appear to be continuous conversations. So that means that there is always an innocent, if you like, explanation possible for these stop signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. That's one possibility. And then, of course, there's the other possibility too, that there's a not-so-innocent explanation for the phenomenon; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: I don't know, because I think it is perfectly legitimate for anyone to make a copy of a telephone conversation and produce a stop signature at the end of it. That is not tampering with the integrity of the conversation; it just means it's a copy at times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go on to the third item, a narrow-band spectrum analysis. Once again, you could do that, but you did not do that; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: I did briefly look at -- but this was again after I received Mr. Koenig's report -- the question of, you know, the multigenerational copies. I assume that that is based partly on the presence or absence of 50 hertz hum, and I have not looked fully or even, you know, begun to look into that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. The fourth item is a spectrographic analysis. Once again, you could have done that, but you didn't, did you?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: I think a spectrographic analysis would not necessarily add a great deal in this particular case, but, you know, it's easy to do it. I mean, there's no particular problem there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, it may be easy to do, but neither you nor your colleagues actually did that kind of analysis, did they?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: The point is that I wonder whether it would have revealed a great deal. In answering the questions that I was asked, I don't think that it would have made any significant contribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. The fifth item is an analysis of the chemical content, if you like, of the tape by doing a ferro-magnetic analysis. But in order to do that, you have to have the original tape, as I understand it, and since we don't have the original tape available, it would have made -- you really couldn't do such a test in this case.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: I wouldn't have done it anyway, because what we have is the best we have, and that might have destroyed even the best we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And then the sixth form of testing is critical listening, and essentially that's what you did?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, another point of convergence, I think, between you and Mr. Koenig is that there are, indeed, many ways to manipulate a tape. I think you've already said that in your direct examination today and we heard the same from Mr. Koenig, and there isn't any dispute on that; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There's no question that audio tapes themselves can be easily cut and spliced, and I think that the result is not detectable on a copy, as we've previously agreed.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: It can be done in ways that are very difficult to detect and even impossible to detect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And in terms of cutting and splicing, it's far easier, rather than doing what the Prosecution suggest to you, and that's create a 30-minute tape conversation using individual words, it's much easier just to take a phrase or a stand-alone sentence and splice it into a tape to make it appear as if it was said during the course of a conversation; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: It's easier than the procedure and the alternative that you mentioned, but it is not easy by any absolute standards, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And when it's done, and presuming it's done competently, the result is not detectable on a copy. I think we've previously agreed to that.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose, you know, it can be done within certain limits.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. In terms of one of the fundamental questions that brings us before the Court today, and that's really authentication -- in a sense, the very reason that the tapes were sent to you and that they were sent to Mr. Koenig -- I think the point to be made, and it's not lost on anybody, is that without the original, no one can really authenticate the copy of a tape as an accurate copy of the original, can they?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: No. There is no scientific way of doing that. But I think there is a parallel here with the question if it's claimed to be an original, in a way, the same problem arises.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: To use a graphic analogy, if I may, it's almost like asking someone, when you have a blood spot, to do an analysis, a DNA analysis of the blood when you actually take a photograph of the blood spot to the doctor. You simply can't do an analysis of the blood without the blood, and a photograph of the blood or a copy of what the blood looks like just won't suffice. Is that a fair analogy?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Well, whether it's fair, I don't know, but whether it's correct, I think I can say that it's not correct. It's not a correct analogy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: I believe, Mr. Sayers, that this question of the difference between the copy and the original is not challenged. So it's not necessary --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think that's correct, Your Honour, and I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: -- and that it is impossible to work, really, to evaluate from the copy. That wasn't challenged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just to see if we agree about some of the advantages of actually having the original, you can actually take a look at the cassette housing to observe any evidence of tampering or pry marks or screw damage. That's one of the comments that's made in Mr. Koenig's article, and I take it you agree that that's one of the benefits of having the original available.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Anybody who is seriously determined to tamper with a cassette would have the sense not to do it that way. I think that is a very unrealistic scenario, because every forensic examiner would be able to immediately spot these telltale signs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. He outlines a number of other benefits. One is that you can inspect the reel in the housing to see whether any changes have been made.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yes. But the point I'm trying to make is that these are not the real risks. The real risks are the types of tampering that can be achieved by very competent individuals. And I've tried to indicate in my report, because I thought that on that particular point I could not entirely agree with Mr. Koenig that his statements, and on that particular point, were potentially misleading to people who do not know, who do not work in the field, who do not know about speech synthesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One of the things that you can -- one of the pieces of valuable information that you can actually derive, though, from looking at the original tape is to look at the batch number that's listed on the tape, and from that you can determine the date of manufacture of the tape; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: From that you can actually see whether, chronologically, it would be possible for the tape actually to have been made at the time of the conversation or not.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know what the date of manufacture of the JPS C-60 tape was?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you were given this JPS C-60 tape. Was there any marking on it to indicate that it had in fact been marked as an exhibit in this trial, an original exhibit?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: I'd have to go back in memory. I think it was clear to me that it was an important piece of evidence and it was treated accordingly. What is unusual in this case, is that when I got to writing my report, I no longer had the actual exhibit in my custody because I had released it earlier. And that explains why I have not given more detail describing the exhibit in my report, simply because I no longer had it physically in the laboratory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was it provided to you in an envelope or jacket or some way to indicate that it had been marked as an exhibit in this case, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: What we do routinely is to check the data in association with exhibits that are provided to us by the police or any prosecutor, and I also remember signing a custody sheet, UN Tribunal custody sheet, when I received the two cassettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was it your understanding that this was an original exhibit, or not?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: I'm a scientist when it comes to these sort of questions, so I do not listen to -- I mean, I don't pay too much attention to what people say, whether it's an original or a copy, because that's the very question. So I can't see how that really matters. I was asked a specific question, but it was described as an original compilation, which is somewhat of a contradiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just enlighten us. What do you mean by that, an "original compilation"?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: I don't know. These are not my words. It was described to me as an original compilation. I was just saying that that is somewhat of a contradiction in terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who was it that described that to you?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: That was the investigator, Ms. Taylor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the Fuji tape, was the same regime applied there?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, they were -- I received them together. Both on same date, same occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You make an observation in your report that it's possible that the Fuji tape was a copy of the JPS tape but equally possible that it was a copy of a brother or parent of the JPS tape.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There's no way to tell, is there?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I think that another point of -- did you actually make a record of the batch number of each one of these tapes anywhere when you were looking at them?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: No, we didn't do that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is it normal practice to do that, or not?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: No. It is -- but this, in a way, is not a normal case, because in the sense that a normal case is one that from the very beginning -- I mean, the question that we were asked was not to write a report but to do a preliminary investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But when you take in audiotapes for forensic analysis in your regular work, Mr. Broeders, I take it that one of the pieces of information that you can ascertain from the tape itself is the batch number, and that it is your regular practice to make a record of that.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: I was referring to that when I said -- when I wrote my report, because I no longer had access to the cassettes, I was unable to add, to specify the batch numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But during the three months that they were in your possession, you didn't make any record of the batch number, I take it?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, another point of convergence, I think, between Mr. Koenig and you is that when you look at these two tapes, it's apparent that there are some differences between them, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: For example, 8.2 seconds of the text that appears on the JPS tape is missing on the Fuji tape; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There are two series of rhythmic signals on the Fuji tape that do not appear on the JPS tape.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You make the observation that maybe these were caused by a cellular phone, or a cellular telephone.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But you're not sure about that, are you?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Well, again you have to be careful here. What we did do in our laboratory was do replication experiments, and we, with a GSM telephone -- this was done by people in the digital technology department at our request, and my colleague was actually -- did actually -- was present at part of the test. What we found was that if -- that in this way the same effect would be reached, okay. So in other words, these signals are consistent with having been produced by a GSM, but there may be other explanations that we didn't look into.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What exactly are you telling us: that while this recording on the Fuji tape was being made, this recording of presumably a tape with important contents on it, someone was calling the person making the tape on a cellular telephone?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: What may have happened was that in the recording process, when the Fuji tape was being recorded, was being made, as it were, a GSM telephone was activated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Going back to the differences between the two tapes, there's an echo on the Fuji tape that does not appear on the JPS tape; is that the case?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yes. It's in my report, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in fact there's a delay of some period of time that's on the Fuji tape that again does not appear on the JPS tape; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: I think the delay -- isn't that the echo?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Five hundred milliseconds, I believe.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yeah, so -- 500 milliseconds. Yeah, that's true. Yes, that's what we found.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And also one other additional difference is that the overall frequency distribution on the Fuji tape contains more lower-frequency energy and less higher-frequency energy than does the JPS tape; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Did anybody at the Prosecution's office let you know that the discrepancy between the conversations that we went to earlier in your cross-examination, the fact that there are 10 conversations and not 11 conversations on side A, and more conversations than are listed on side B on the JPS tape. Did anyone tell you that that was actually the subject of a memorandum from one of the lawyers in the Prosecution to another of the lawyers in the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- making a point about the fact that there was a discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, sir. I do not have any other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, sir, we don't have any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A few things arising, please. The scientific side of the work, does that require any more scientific abilities than you have or is it well within your capability? What's the position?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Well, I think that's difficult for me to judge, but what I have done -- I'm a member of -- I'm actually the chairman of the NC European Network of Forensic Science Institute's Working Group for speech and audio analysis, and not only in that capacity, but in other capacities as well, we often discuss case work with colleagues, with foreign colleagues. So I know how, for example, my British colleagues do their authenticity integrity work, and in that sense I think I can say that we do more or less the same things as they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you given evidence here before?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: In this Tribunal, no, but I've written a report. But I've never been asked to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you've been asked a lot of questions about what you were told and what you were asked to deal with, and you've explained that you were asked to provide a preliminary report. Just tell us, is the purity of a scientist's results sometimes assisted by simply being left with the raw material to work on?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Well, there's always the danger of bias, if that is possibly what you're referring to, in the sense that the more information as a scientist you receive, the more room there is for bias. On the other hand, in order to do an examination properly, you have to really usually work with a hypothesis or with a number of hypotheses, and you can test these hypotheses. If there's no hypothesis, it's very difficult to do a useful examination that will lead to usable results.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, that brings me directly, I was going to come to it later, but that brings me directly to the questions you've been asked by Mr. Sayers. Mr. Sayers has at no point suggested to you that this particular sentence or this particular phrase could have been corrupted by taking this clause and that clause, has he?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If that had been done, if that sort of proposition had been put to you, might you have been able to assist the Chamber with the possibility or probability of such an exercise being successful?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: I think it's -- would also require expertise in the original language of the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: But at least it would be a testable hypothesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you were asked by -- who was it, by Ms. Taylor for a preliminary report?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You subsequently spoke to me, I can't remember when exactly, but if your records show you can tell us. But between the time when you spoke to Ms. Taylor and the time when you spoke to me, had you been privy at all to whatever particular strategy or purpose I was ensuing in having a preliminary report. Did you know one way or the other what I was after?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: I was -- the impression I got was, and I suppose I was also told that these four conversations were more important than the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: And that it would be possible for the Defence to try and argue that these were not integral uninterrupted recordings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there any urgency? You made an oral report to Ms. Taylor or someone else?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: To Ms. Taylor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was that to the effect that there was or was not any effect of tampering?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: It was to the effect that there was no evidence in the four conversations that I had concentrated on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Between making those -- that oral report and receipt of Mr. Koenig's report, were you under any pressure of time to produce a written report or anything else?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The rhythmic signals, by the way, do you know one way or the other whether that can be produced by mere presence in proximity to a GSM telephone?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't be qualified to testify on that because that was explicitly done by somebody in the digital technology department and I think it would not be correct for me to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been asked a number of factual things about what other witnesses may have said. There's only one I'm going to deal with because it's really outside of your area, but you were asked about the use of microcassettes. If a witness said -- 13698 is the page number -- no, you won't have it, don't worry. The equipment switched on to that particular office allowed surveyance on the basis of an interphone and there was a microcassette recorder, a microtape recorder which was switched on to that appliance. Does that trigger any recollection of the sort of use that might be made of microcassettes or not?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: There may have been -- I don't know the context in which the tapes were made or allegedly recorded, but it might have been a telephone taping facility. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've got your waveform analyses or some form in the bag with you, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: I've got a number of plots of the part of the first conversation in particular which help me simply identify, locate certain utterances in the conversation which I felt were important and helped me sort of follow my way through the recording more specifically. Because in this first recording, it's only after 50 seconds from the beginning of the recording that the two progatonists are introduced. So the first 50 seconds are apparently taken up by other people setting up the connection, as it were, between those two speakers. And also to locate, for example, the busy signal at the end of what appears to be the first telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Along that topic, or on a connected topic, although as His Honour said, the question of the number of phone calls on a tape, on an index is really not necessarily a matter for you, but as you make clear in your report when you deal with the tapes that you were asked to examine, and that's another question I want to ask you about, you make it clear that there is, as it were, an ambiguity as to whether you include them as two conversations or one?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yes. On my report in section 3.1.3.2, I write that I think conversations one, five, eight and ten occur as part of what appear to be part of calls one, five, seven and nine. So, in other words, telephone call seven appears to consist of two separate conversations. In other words, half-way through that conversation, it looks as though the phone is passed on to another person so that all together there are three people. One pair of speakers and then one of these speakers presumably passes on the phone to another speaker, and these are recorded apparently as separate conversations which, in fact, they are, except they are not telephone conversations presumably on the inlay card which explains some of the oddity, possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I think I've only got a couple more questions, and those are these: On stop signals, if the Chamber wanted you to do it, or if indeed I did, would you be able to do the whole analysis and if Mr. Koenig would provide his charts, which he hasn't provided fully in the report, would you be prepared to look at those?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Given time, that would be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed would you be possible to cooperate with Mr. Koenig if that would help the Chamber more as well?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where tapes were produced, for example, to Mr. Koenig in the process of copying, do you know one way or another, whether stop signals would have been left on the tape in that process simply in providing them to him to listen to?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: That's possible but, again, I wasn't there. So if it was done with a degree, a minimum degree of competence, that shouldn't happen but you never know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. And -- yes, I mean you haven't again being asked about this but -- do you remember -- this is my last question you haven't been asked specifically but in general, Mr. Koenig, in his answers to me expressed views in agreement with my questions to him about the limited possibilities for piecing together conversations, do you agree with what he said about that?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIUS PETRUS ARNOLDUS BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yes. I think I do. But again, I find that what I've written down in my report is preferably what I would stick to because I find it more difficult to express these things, to write them down is easier than to express them orally. So I would rather not make a less precise statement than I've made in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, subject to further assistance that the expert could give the Court, I may just refer to that briefly after he's withdrawn so as in no way to affect anything he might say, that's all I ask of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Broeders, thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. It is now concluded. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the Court's permission, could Mr. Koenig leave too? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nice, the state of the evidence is this, that there is an application to exclude this tape --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- made by the Defence. At an appropriate moment, that must be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, I don't know whether there's any application by either party for further submissions. In the light of the evidence which has been given today, they may want to consider that. And if they want to make further submissions then, of course, you can, it might be a sensible way of looking at it. And then before the close of Mr. Kordic's case, we ought to rule on the matter. That is my suggested programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can deal with that before -- at any time, I'm happy with that. There is quite a lot to be said about the tape one way or another. I won't forecast any arguments on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry to interrupt. There is one aspect of it unless anybody wants to call any more evidence about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's really what I was going to touch on and to some extent, I think it's helpful to remind the Chamber of just one or two features of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me confer, I'm sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the matter that we were considering was this, and no doubt you would have had it in mind yourself as to whether Mr. Husic should be recalled in order that specific matters should be put to him relating to the possibility of contamination or indeed a deliberate splicing, if that is going to be the suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think Your Honour was ahead of me in what I was going to raise, and I was just going to make two points at this stage of the longish history, and I'll deal with them in reverse order. First, there having been an allegation raised, however incompletely and unsatisfactorily, the reason that the tapes were sent to this witness at an early stage in the absence of any detail from the Defence was to ensure that if there was any reason to doubt them, I wouldn't rely on them in cross-examination. And I had nothing from the Defence that I needed to be sure, as far as I could be, that it was proper to rely on. That's why we had an oral report and waited for details. And so that was my purpose, and a very proper purpose too. Now, coming back to the earlier matter, Your Honours hit on a matter of history and that I was going to raise in any event. Because the witness wasn't just a producer of the tape, he produced a great deal, gave a great deal of evidence authenticating the tapes and the conversations he heard and identifying the speakers, and I raised with the Court twice that the cross-examination was woefully inadequate and should have been dealt with properly and fully. And Your Honour can find the end of this on 13916 of the transcript where, having raised it on the 4th of February, I think for the second time, Your Honour suggested to Mr. Stein who was dealing with it, that if there were matters he wanted to draw to your attention which he normally would have done through cross-examination, he should do so and do so fairly soon. In fact, nothing more was heard from them. The matter was simply left waiting, eventually, for Mr. Koenig's report, and that's been one of the problems with this case. The matter has never properly been joined. I have no objection at all to Mr. Husic coming back and there may be other witnesses as well who would follow in his train if and when the matter is properly joined, and indeed I raise the possibility of other witnesses as well at an earlier stage saying, well, if this is going to be pursued seriously, let's hear about it, because we can't just have a sort of general smear allegation and so on. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think you can take it, and there's no point going back to the Defence, in my view, now, you can take it that this is an issue which has been raised. The suggestion is that this is a falsified document and it might as well be faced. The question is when will it be appropriate to deal with it whether the normal course of events would be to deal with, it would seem to me, during your rebuttal case, but we'll bear in mind issues timing and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I was going to raise it again in relation to the suggestion that somehow there was a ration of rebuttal time from which this should be deducted, because that would be quite wrong given that the issue should have been raised and fully when the witness was here and not left. I would invite the Court to let us find out how available the witness is and if there is a time that he could conveniently be fitted in, really at any time, because it's a free-standing issue, let's have him back and fit him in in order to certainly avoid to adding on to the pressures of time later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll consider that. Perhaps you can find out from the witness when he's available, then we'll consider an appropriate time. Mr. Sayers, I'm not going to ask you. The matter was raised, it was dealt with in a very, if I may say, a very equivocal way by the Defence, but it seems to me that you have now raised the issue as to whether this is an authentic tape and you are making the suggestion, it may not be directly, but by implication, that you don't accept that it's original, but it is open to have been the tampered with or manufactured in some way. Now, unless you accept that it's authentic, it seems to me that we have to pursue the matter with the witness, and he must be given the opportunity of dealing with the suggestion. Unless there's something you want to say about that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do not see how we could possibly accept the two tapes that have been introduced into evidence as authentic. They're not, and also other than the testimony of Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, is the Prosecutor now arguing that these tapes are authentic tapes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A question of terminology. They are not the original tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Without any alteration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do they represent the conversation as recorded, that's the crucial question, and the Prosecution say it is; Defence say not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think that's an accurate depiction of our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It seems to me in those circumstances we shall have to hear from the witness again so that he has the opportunity of dealing with it and we'll have to consider his convenience amongst other things and then deciding when he should be called. Now, unless there are any other matters, that's -- concludes the hearing for today. Half past nine tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
